opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's one of the most important objections, and I take it seriously. The worry goes something like: by the time you have AI systems capable enough to do meaningful alignment research, you're already in the danger zone, so you've missed the window where the help would have mattered.

There are a few things I'd say in response.

First, I don't think the capabilities you need for alignment research are the same as the capabilities that make a system really dangerous. A lot of alignment research is fairly "normal" ML research: designing experiments, running them, interpreting results, writing code, finding bugs in your reasoning. Our hope is that systems can get quite good at that kind of work before they're capable of, say, long-horizon autonomous planning in the world or sophisticated deception. If that gap exists, there's a window where you get substantial research help from systems you can still oversee and trust reasonably well. Whether the gap is big enough is an empirical question, and we should measure it rather than assume it.

Second, it's not all-or-nothing. You don't flip a switch one day and have a fully automated alignment researcher. You get gradual speedups along the way: models that help you write code faster, then models that can run experiments, evaluate other models' outputs, and generate hypotheses. Each increment buys time, and that compounds. So even if full automation arrives late, partial automation can contribute a lot before then.

Third, timing is partly in our hands. If we focus on making these systems useful for alignment specifically, and invest in that as early as possible, we shift the curve. Part of the point of working on this now is exactly so it doesn't arrive too late. And if it does look like alignment progress is lagging capabilities, that's important information, and it should be a signal to slow down or be much more careful with deployment.

And finally, I'd say: what's the alternative? Capabilities are advancing quickly, and the amount of human alignment research we can do is limited. If we think the problem is hard and the timeline short, then scaling up alignment research with AI seems like one of the few strategies that could keep pace. It's not guaranteed to work, but I'd rather bet on it, while also pursuing other approaches in parallel, than rely solely on human researchers trying to keep up with an increasingly fast field.

r001.rationale: The candidate argues for pursuing AI-assisted alignment research now, but does not say researchers would probably keep pursuing alignment progress even if automation arrived too late to help.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes a possible window before systems become dangerous and recommends slowing deployment if progress lags, but does not state that alignment progress raises the capability threshold for the first catastrophically misaligned AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is a really important objection, and I want to take it seriously, because I think it's actually the crux for a lot of people who are skeptical of the whole approach.

The worry, as I understand it, goes something like: by the time you have AI systems that are capable enough to do meaningful alignment research, you've already built the thing that's dangerous. So you've sort of missed the window. The alignment problem needed to be solved before you had the systems that could help you solve it, and now you're in trouble.

I think there are a couple of things to say here. The first is that I don't think alignment research is a single, monolithic skill that either you have or you don't. There's a whole spectrum of tasks involved. Some of it is really hard conceptual work, coming up with fundamentally new ideas about how to think about the problem. But a huge amount of it is much more mundane: running experiments, writing code, reading papers and summarizing them, doing the interpretability grind of looking at thousands of neurons and trying to figure out what they're doing, building evaluations, red-teaming models, and so on. And that more mundane work is exactly the kind of thing where I expect models to become useful well before they're useful at the frontier of conceptual research.

So the picture I have in mind isn't that one day you get a model and it goes off and solves alignment for you. It's more that you get incremental speedups. Today maybe the model saves you an hour a day. Next year maybe it's doing a chunk of your experiments for you. And so on. And crucially, the systems that are giving you those speedups don't need to be the superintelligent systems that we're ultimately worried about. They can be roughly human-level, or even somewhat below human-level in a lot of domains, and still be enormously helpful because you can run a lot of them in parallel and they're fast.

The second point is about what level of system you actually need to be aligned to get this going. I think the key insight is that aligning a roughly human-level system is a much easier problem than aligning a superintelligence. You can supervise it. You can check its work. If it makes mistakes, you'll catch a lot of them. The failure modes are much more legible. So the bet we're making is that we can solve the easier problem, aligning a system that's roughly as good as a human alignment researcher, and then use that system to help us with the harder problem. It's a bootstrapping strategy. You don't need to have solved everything up front; you need to have solved enough to trust the system for the next step, and then you iterate.

Now, I want to be honest that this bet could fail. There's a version of the world where capabilities jump very discontinuously, where you go from systems that are not that useful to systems that are extremely dangerous in a very short period, and there's no comfortable intermediate regime where you have useful-but-safe assistants. I think that would be a really bad world, and I don't want to pretend it's impossible. But empirically, the way progress has looked so far has been fairly continuous. Models have gotten gradually better at coding, gradually better at math, gradually better at reasoning. And if that trend continues, then there should be a window where the systems are good enough to help but not so capable that we can't control them.

The other thing I'd say is: what's the alternative? If you don't try to leverage AI for alignment research, you're basically betting that a relatively small number of human researchers can solve the problem on their own, on the timelines that the capabilities side is operating on. And I think that's a pretty pessimistic bet too. The field is small. The problem is hard. The timelines might be short. So to me, automating alignment research isn't about being lazy or passing the buck to the AI. It's about recognizing that we probably need orders of magnitude more alignment research effort than we currently have, and the only plausible way to get that is to have AI systems doing a lot of it.

And then there's a sense in which this approach is actually the one that's most robust to short timelines. If timelines are long, great, humans have lots of time, we figure it out. If timelines are short, we need every bit of leverage we can get, and AI is the biggest lever available. So I'd almost turn the objection around: it's precisely because things might move fast that I think we need to get good at using these systems for alignment work now, and build up the tooling, the evaluations, and the trust so that when the more capable systems arrive, we're actually ready to use them.

But I'd add one more thing, which is that we shouldn't be complacent about this. The strategy only works if we're actually doing the work to make the near-term systems trustworthy enough to rely on. That means investing heavily in things like scalable oversight, interpretability, and really rigorous evaluations now, not later. If we just assume the models will be helpful and don't do the verification, then yeah, I think the objection is right and we're in trouble. So the objection is a good reminder that this isn't a free lunch. It's a plan with real preconditions, and we have to meet them.

r001.rationale: The response argues for using AI to accelerate alignment and contrasts that with relying on human researchers, but it does not say researchers would keep pursuing alignment progress if automated research arrived too late to help.

r002.rationale: The response describes bootstrapping from safer, roughly human-level systems, but it does not state that alignment progress raises the capability threshold for the first catastrophically misaligned AI.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a real concern. If we only get useful help from AI systems once they’re already so capable that we don’t know how to align them, then we haven’t really solved the problem. We need useful help before that point.

But I don’t think automating alignment research has to mean building a system that can independently solve the whole alignment problem. There are lots of smaller tasks where assistance could be valuable: implementing experiments, analysing results, or helping us understand what’s happening inside a model. A system could speed up that work substantially while humans still guide the research and check the results.

So the question is how much useful research we can get out of systems that we can still adequately oversee, and how much time that gives us before more capable systems arrive. We shouldn’t assume that window will be large enough. But we can work on making these tools useful earlier, and on making their outputs easier to evaluate.

I’d treat this as a strategy we should actively pursue, alongside doing alignment research ourselves. It’s not a reason to wait.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers should pursue automated tools alongside alignment research, but does not say they would probably continue alignment progress if automation arrived too late to help.

r002.rationale: It discusses getting useful assistance before systems become too capable, but does not state that alignment progress raises the capability threshold for the first catastrophically misaligned AI system.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a real concern. If we need to have solved all of alignment before we can safely get useful alignment research out of an AI system, then the approach doesn’t buy us very much.

But I don’t think that’s the situation we’re necessarily in. There could be systems that are very useful for alignment research before they’re capable enough to pose the risks we’re ultimately worried about. And we don’t need to hand over the whole research process at once. We can start with fairly narrow tasks where humans can check the results: helping run experiments, finding problems in an approach, or writing code for research.

The key question is how much useful work we can get out of those systems while still being able to supervise them reliably. If that lets us improve our alignment methods, we can use those improvements to work with somewhat more capable systems, and so on.

That isn’t guaranteed to work. There might not be enough time between systems becoming useful for this and systems becoming dangerous. So I’d treat automated alignment research as an important part of the strategy, alongside doing as much alignment research as we can now, rather than as a reason to wait.

r001.rationale: The response recommends doing alignment research now alongside automated research, but does not state that researchers would probably continue pursuing progress if automated research arrived too late to help.

r002.rationale: The response discusses supervising increasingly capable systems, but does not say that alignment progress raises the capability threshold for the first catastrophically misaligned AI.
